A.best_thing: Compute cells, not buffers: each op gives one cell's value from the whole-grid formula in absolute coordinates, and a sparse memo of computed cells makes overlap sharing and exactness come for free.
A.worst_thing: An unbounded per-cell dict cache that only reset_counters can clear; on a 6000x4000 scan a few whole-node requests fill memory with Python tuples.

generativity.notes: Every implementation converged on the same core: declared footprint, clip to extent, absolute coordinates, border from the whole extent. They split on the unit of work. A and E compute cells into a sparse absolute-keyed store. That gives sharing for overlapping windows, and a short footprint becomes a crash, not silent drift, so they never needed a guard. B, C and D compute window buffers. They needed an explicit guard and an explicit statistic node, and they differ only in caching: none in B, the statistic only in C, optional and off by default in D. Within the groups, A's cache persists across calls (spans) while E's lasts one request (two-phase demand/compute). D is B/C plus every optional participant. Up2 in NEXT.md exposes a common gap: none has an inverse-map helper with floor/ceil rounding, because half was mapped back by multiplication alone in every implementation.

worse_is_better: C reaches D's quality on the forces this task has: an explicit guard on sources, a split and cached statistic, and fresh-engine invariance tests, in about 650 library lines against D's 880. It does without D's cost rule, optional whole cache, per-request memo, spec/describe/KIND/REACH metadata, two-layer Buffer+Guarded and in-package invariance checker. None of those is needed: the demo ops are cheap per cell, the cost rule and cache are off in demo_engine, and REACH duplicates footprint(). B is smaller still, but it shows where 'less' becomes too little: without C's few lines of statistic caching, every normalize window recomputes a whole grid. In the other group, E reaches A's sharing and exactness without A's interval-merging _Spans and its unbounded cross-call cache.
chapter_lessons: The chapter treats storage as tiles or windows, but the code shows a third option it should name. A per-cell sparse store keyed by absolute coordinates (A, E) gives overlap sharing without a tile grid. It also turns the chapter's main risk, a short footprint that fails silently at window edges, into a crash, because an uncomputed cell simply is not there. The footprint guard is needed only for dense, offset-addressed buffers (B, C, D).

Tie the statistic split to its cache explicitly. B and D split normalize into a max node and a divide, but without a cache they recompute the max and its whole input for every window (1227 cells against 412-425 for A, C, E on three windows). The split matters for windows only if the statistic's whole value is kept.

Mark the optional participants (cost rule, whole cache, tiles, self-describing reach metadata) as optional with a test for when to build them. D built them all, off by default, with only tests as callers, and its REACH metadata duplicates footprint().
Give the rounding rule for inverse maps: floor the start, ceil the end. Every implementation mapped half back by multiplication and none has a helper that up2 (or any non-integer resample) can reuse.

Say that 'exact' means equal to the fixed whole-grid definition, not only to the engine's own whole run, and test against an independent reference with ==. C reordered summation for speed, stayed window-equals-whole, but drifted from the task formula and loosened its tests to isclose.

Note 1's warning that caches hide footprint errors needs a concrete rule: evaluate each test window on a fresh engine. A's per-op window test reuses one engine and asks for the whole extent first (impl-A/tests/test_windows.py:43-56), so every later window is served from cache.
